title: Boss: get me out of here
summary: Rescue a stuck colleague, recover a crashed edit from a swap file, and walk away without damage.

steps.title: A colleague is stuck
body: Three real messes, each from a call you will get one day:
1. *"I typed `:wq` and it just appeared in the file."* They were still in Insert mode.
2. *"My SSH dropped while I was editing, and now Vim shows `E325: ATTENTION`."* A **swap file** (`.name.swp`) holds the unsaved edits.
3. *"I made a mess, I just want out, nothing saved."*
The first and third are keys (in the trainer). The second is real Vim on a real file.

> **Swap files:** Vim writes your unsaved changes to `.file.swp` every few seconds. When it finds one at startup it shows E325 and offers (O)pen read-only, (E)dit anyway, (R)ecover, (D)elete it, (Q)uit. Recover, check, `:w`, then delete the swap file, or E325 comes back every time.

steps.title: :wq in the file
prompt: The level starts the way your colleague left it: still in Insert mode, with `:wq` typed at the end of their new line.
Keep their `restart: always` line, remove the `:wq` junk, then save and quit for real.
steps.explain: Always look at the bottom line first. `-- INSERT --` means every key is text. `Esc` is the way back to Normal mode from almost anywhere; pressing it twice never hurts.

steps.title: E325: recover the lost edit
prompt: Your SSH session dropped while you were editing `~/notes/oncall.md`. The line you added (`- 02:25 rotated /var/log/app, 40 GB freed`) was never saved, but Vim's swap file `~/notes/.oncall.md.swp` has it.
1. Recover the edit into `oncall.md`. `vim -r file` recovers from the swap file; here use it in Ex mode: `vim -Nes -r oncall.md -c ...`.
2. Delete the swap file, so the next person who opens the file does not get E325.
`ls -a ~/notes` shows the swap file; `cat` it and you will see it is binary, which is why you let Vim read it.

checks.name: oncall.md has the recovered line
checks.fail: `oncall.md` does not have the lost line yet (or has something extra). `vim -Nes -r oncall.md -c 'w!' -c q` recovers and writes it.

checks.name: the swap file is gone
checks.fail: The swap file is still there. Vim does not delete it after a recovery; `rm ~/notes/.oncall.md.swp` once the file is saved.

checks.name: no Vim is left running
checks.fail: A Vim process is still running. Type `q!` and Enter in it, or `pkill vim`.

hints: `ls -a ~/notes` shows `.oncall.md.swp`. `vim -r oncall.md` is "open oncall.md, recovering from its swap file".
In Ex mode: `cd ~/notes && vim -Nes -r oncall.md -c 'w!' -c q`. Check with `cat oncall.md`.
steps.explain: Recover, look, write, delete the swap: in that order. Deleting the swap first throws the edits away; writing without deleting it brings back E325 forever. In full-screen Vim: open the file, press `R` at the E325 prompt, check the text, `:w`, then `:!rm .oncall.md.swp` (or answer `D` the next time).

steps.title: Out, nothing saved
prompt: Someone typed junk into a config and did not save. Quit **without** saving, so the file on disk stays clean. `:q` will refuse (E37); you know the way round it.
steps.explain: `:q!` (or `ZQ`) throws away every unsaved change. The file on disk is exactly what it was.
